steps: Read the key to understand symbol sizes
Compare symbols to the scale to estimate values
Flow lines: note width (volume) and direction (arrow)
Identify spatial patterns and dominant flows
method_card.title: Proportional Symbol & Flow Line Maps
method_card.content:
Proportional symbol maps use symbols (usually circles) whose size is proportional to the value they represent. Larger circles mean higher values — for example, larger circles for cities with bigger populations. The area of the circle (not the radius) should be proportional to the value, so a city twice as populous should have a circle with twice the area, not twice the diameter.

Flow line maps use arrows or lines whose width is proportional to the volume of movement — such as migration flows, trade volumes, or traffic counts. Thicker arrows mean more movement. The direction of the arrow shows where the flow goes.

To read these maps: (1) study the key/scale — it will show reference sizes (e.g. a circle representing 1 million people), (2) compare symbol sizes visually or use the scale to estimate values, (3) look for spatial patterns.

Advantages: Both show location-specific data clearly and allow quick visual comparison. Limitations: Large symbols can overlap and obscure each other; flow lines can become tangled in areas with many connections; exact values are hard to read without a precise scale.
method_card.example:
Proportional symbol example: A map shows city populations with circles. The key shows: small circle = 100,000, medium circle = 500,000, large circle = 1,000,000. City X has a circle roughly halfway between medium and large, so its estimated population is around 750,000.

Flow line example: A migration map shows arrows between countries. The arrow from Mexico to the USA is 5 mm wide, and the key shows 1 mm = 50,000 people per year. So the estimated flow is 5 × 50,000 = 250,000 migrants per year.

gold.display: Using the flow line map, calculate the total migration flow into London from Birmingham (60,000), Manchester (45,000), and Leeds (30,000). Give your answer in thousands.

misconceptions.message: 60 + 45 + 30 = 135 thousand total inward migration to London from these three cities.

gold.display: A student draws a proportional symbol map but makes the radius of each circle proportional to the value, instead of the area. London (population 8.8 million) gets a circle with 10 times the radius of Newcastle (300,000). Why is this misleading?
options: The circles should all be the same size
Using radius instead of area makes London appear 100 times larger than Newcastle, massively exaggerating the difference
Proportional symbols should use squares, not circles
Newcastle is actually larger than London

misconceptions.message: Area increases with the square of the radius. A circle with 10x the radius has 100x the area, making the visual difference far greater than the actual data difference (about 29x). The area, not the radius, should be proportional.

gold.display: The map shows red arrows from London to Bristol and Manchester. This movement away from London is an example of which geographical process?
options: Urbanisation
Counter-urbanisation
Suburbanisation
Gentrification

misconceptions.message: Counter-urbanisation is the movement of people away from large cities to smaller cities or rural areas, often driven by lower house prices, better quality of life, and remote working.

gold.display: Evaluate the proportional symbol map as a way of showing UK city populations. Which statement best describes its strengths and weaknesses?
options: It shows exact values clearly but cannot show location
It shows the spatial distribution and relative size of cities at a glance, but exact values are hard to read and symbols overlap in crowded areas
It is better than a bar chart in every way
It only works for capital cities

misconceptions.message: Proportional symbol maps excel at showing WHERE data is and HOW MUCH in one visual. Weaknesses: exact values hard to read from circle sizes, overlap in dense areas, and large symbols can obscure the base map.

gold.display: A student wants to improve this flow line map. Which suggestion would be most useful?
options: Remove all the arrows and just use a table
Add exact figures as labels on each arrow so readers can see both the pattern and precise values
Make all arrows the same width for fairness
Only show flows to London and remove all other arrows

misconceptions.message: Adding data labels combines the visual advantage of flow lines (direction and relative size) with the precision of exact figures. This addresses the main weakness of flow line maps.

bronze.display: Look at the proportional symbol map. Which city has the largest population?
options: Birmingham
Manchester
London
Glasgow

misconceptions.message: The largest circle represents the largest population. London has by far the biggest circle on the map.

bronze.display: On the flow line map, which city sends the most migrants to London?
options: Manchester
Leeds
Birmingham
Liverpool

misconceptions.message: The thickest blue arrow going to London comes from Birmingham (60,000 per year). Thicker arrows = larger flows.

bronze.display: Using the map and key, which of these cities has a population closest to 500,000?
options: London
Birmingham
Liverpool
Norwich

misconceptions.message: Compare circle sizes to the key. The 500 (thousands) reference circle matches Liverpool (498,000) most closely.

bronze.display: The flow line map uses two colours. What do the red arrows represent?
options: Migration towards London
Migration away from London
International migration
Commuter journeys

misconceptions.message: The key shows red = from London. The red arrows point away from London towards Bristol and Manchester.

bronze.display: Birmingham has the second-largest circle on the map. Using the key, estimate its population.
options: About 500,000

misconceptions.message: Birmingham's circle is between the 500 and 2,000 key circles, closer to 500. The population is approximately 1,000,000 (1,145,000).

bronze.display: Which of these datasets would be best shown using a proportional symbol map?
options: Average temperature across UK regions
Number of hospital beds in each city
Percentage of land used for farming by county
Direction of wind across the country

misconceptions.message: Proportional symbol maps are ideal for showing totals or counts at specific locations (like hospital beds per city). Percentages suit choropleths; direction suits flow lines.

bronze.display: Compare the blue arrow from Leeds to London with the blue arrow from Birmingham to London. What can you conclude?
options: More people migrate from Leeds than from Birmingham
More people migrate from Birmingham than from Leeds
Equal numbers migrate from both cities
The arrows show commuter journeys, not migration

misconceptions.message: The arrow from Birmingham is thicker than the one from Leeds. Thicker = larger volume. Birmingham sends 60,000 vs Leeds 30,000.

bronze.display: Give one advantage of a flow line map over a table of migration figures.
options: A flow line map shows exact numbers more precisely
A flow line map shows the direction and relative size of movements at a glance
A flow line map can display more data than a table
Tables cannot show migration data

misconceptions.message: Flow line maps show both direction (where arrows point) and volume (arrow width) visually, making patterns immediately obvious. Tables show exact numbers but patterns are harder to spot.

silver.display: The key shows that a circle representing 2,000,000 people has roughly twice the diameter of one representing 500,000 people. Glasgow and Edinburgh have similar-sized circles. Using the key, estimate Glasgow's population in thousands.

misconceptions.message: Glasgow's circle is slightly larger than the 500 key circle. Its population is approximately 636,000.

silver.display: The flow from Birmingham to London is 60,000 people per year. The flow from Leeds to London appears to be half as wide. Estimate the Leeds to London flow in thousands.

misconceptions.message: If the Birmingham arrow (60,000) is twice the width, then Leeds is approximately 60,000 ÷ 2 = 30,000.

silver.display: In the area around Manchester, Leeds, Sheffield, and Liverpool, the circles are close together. What problem does this create for the map reader?
options: The colours are too similar
Circles overlap, making it hard to read individual values
The cities are too far apart to compare
The key does not include these cities

misconceptions.message: When many locations are close together, their proportional symbols can overlap, making it difficult to distinguish individual values. This is a key limitation of proportional symbol maps.

silver.display: The flow from Manchester to London is 45,000 per year. The flow from London to Manchester is 20,000 per year. Calculate the net migration from Manchester to London.

misconceptions.message: Net migration = inflow minus outflow. Manchester to London (45,000) minus London to Manchester (20,000) = 25,000 net movement towards London.

silver.display: Describe the spatial pattern shown by the proportional symbol map.
options: Large cities are evenly spread across the UK
The largest cities are concentrated in the south-east and the Midlands, with smaller cities in Scotland and Wales
All cities have similar populations
Cities in Scotland are larger than cities in England

misconceptions.message: London dominates in the south-east, with a cluster of medium-large cities in the Midlands and north of England. Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland have smaller circles.

silver.display: Most blue arrows on the map point towards London. Suggest a reason for this pattern.
options: London has better weather than other cities
London offers more job opportunities, higher wages, and more services, attracting migrants from across the UK
People prefer to live in the south because it is flatter
London is the only city with universities

misconceptions.message: London is a global city with the UK's highest concentration of employment, services, and cultural opportunities. This creates a strong pull factor for internal migration.

silver.display: A student wants to show both the total population of UK cities and the population density of the regions around them. Which combination of map types would work best?
options: Two choropleth maps
A proportional symbol map for city totals and a choropleth for regional density
Two flow line maps
A dot map and a flow line map

misconceptions.message: Proportional symbols show totals at points (city populations). Choropleths show ratios across areas (density). Together they show both dimensions.

steps.label: Calculate
steps.content: 3 cm = 3 × 2 million = 6 million (note: this is a simplified linear scale — true proportional symbols scale by area)

worked_examples.question: On a proportional symbol map, the key shows a circle with diameter 1 cm = 2 million people. City A has a circle with diameter 3 cm. Estimate its population.
A flow line map shows trade between countries. Arrow from UK to USA is 8 mm wide, and the scale shows 2 mm = £10 billion. Calculate the estimated trade value.
